questions.prompt: What actually causes Earth to have seasons?
options: Earth moving closer to and farther from the Sun
Earth's axis staying tilted in the same direction as it orbits the Sun
The Moon blocking sunlight for part of the year
Earth's rotation speeding up and slowing down
questions.explanation: Earth's 23.5° axial tilt stays pointed the same direction all year, so different points in the orbit put different hemispheres closer to facing the Sun directly. That changing angle — not changing distance — is what drives seasons.
questions.misconception: Earth's distance from the Sun barely changes across the year, and in the Northern Hemisphere the closest approach actually happens in January — the middle of winter. Distance is a tempting but wrong explanation.

questions.prompt: During the Northern Hemisphere's summer, what season is the Southern Hemisphere having?
options: Summer too
Winter
Spring
The same as the North, just later
questions.explanation: Because the two hemispheres lean opposite ways relative to the Sun at any given moment, they always have opposite seasons — Northern summer is always Southern winter.
questions.misconception: It's easy to assume the whole planet shares one season, but the tilt affects the North and South oppositely at the exact same time.

questions.prompt: What would happen to seasons if Earth had zero axial tilt?
options: Seasons would be more extreme
Seasons would disappear almost entirely
Only the equator would have seasons
Nothing would change
questions.explanation: With no tilt, no hemisphere would ever lean toward or away from the Sun — every day would look roughly like an equinox everywhere, and seasons would essentially vanish.
questions.misconception: Tilt is easy to overlook since it never seems to "do" anything by itself — but it is the entire cause of the yearly light-and-temperature cycle we call seasons.

questions.prompt: At the equinoxes, what is true almost everywhere on Earth?
options: It is always summer
Day and night are close to equal length
One hemisphere gets no sunlight at all
Earth's rotation temporarily stops
questions.explanation: At an equinox, neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so the sunlit half of Earth splits almost evenly between day and night everywhere — hence the name "equinox," meaning "equal night."
questions.misconception: Solstices (the tilt at its most extreme) are often confused with equinoxes (the tilt at its most neutral) — they are opposite points in the yearly cycle.

options: The day the Northern Hemisphere leans most toward the Sun, giving it the longest day of the year
The single day each year with no sunlight anywhere
The moment Earth is closest to the Sun
Another name for the March equinox
questions.explanation: The June solstice is the point in Earth's orbit where the Northern Hemisphere's lean toward the Sun is at its maximum, giving the North its longest day and the South its shortest.
questions.misconception: Solstices are sometimes assumed to be about Earth's distance from the Sun (like a close-approach event), but they're purely about tilt angle — Earth's Sun distance barely changes at all around a solstice.
